s08.slug: THURSDAY · 9:35 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE, SOL’S DARKROOM
s08.music: The Velvet Underground & Nico — “I’ll Be Your Mirror”
body: The porch light is off and the front door is on the latch, which at Sol’s means come in. Upstairs, Tomás’s door is shut. Somebody two streets over is having Thursday, and it comes through the walls of the house as bass and nothing else, a pulse in the plaster. The downstairs hall runs from the kitchen, where the light over the stove is on and the kettle sits in it, past the foot of the stairs, to the back of the house, where the door he has walked past all winter is shut on a red line of light along the floor.
He knocks.
“Wait —” Quick, through the wood, and a slosh, and a lid going down on a box. “Okay.”
He gets in and gets the door shut behind him faster than he has ever shut a door in his life, and stands with his back against it.
Inside, there are two colors, and one of them is black.

The safelight hangs on its cord over the wet side and makes everything it touches red and gives everything it doesn’t to the dark. The room was a sleeping porch once; he can tell by the windows that aren’t there anymore, plywood where they used to be and blackout cloth stapled over the plywood, and the ceiling sloping down toward the yard. Along the right wall, a utility sink, and three trays in a row on a counter of bare plywood, and a sour bite of vinegar he knows from the peppers in Nonna’s cellar. Along the left, the dry side: old Formica, the enlarger standing on its column with its head bowed, a box of paper with its lid on, and a turntable with a record going around, a woman singing low and level over a guitar, no hurry in her anywhere. On a shelf above the trays a darkroom timer ticks off whatever she has set it for. Overhead, corner to corner, a clothesline, with prints hanging from it by wooden clothespins and dripping on the boards. Under the line, against the back wall where the porch railing must have been, at the end of the dry counter, an iron daybed with a moving blanket thrown over the mattress.

body.title: Taped inside the darkroom door, in marker
body.text: SKYE — DON’T TOUCH: The enlarger lens. The Nikon’s light meter (it lies. I know. Leave it). The box that says FIBER. My negatives. The fuse box (not yours either). CLOSE THE PAPER BEFORE THE DOOR. The daybed is not a shelf. — SOL

body: Skye is at the trays in a black rubber apron over a T-shirt, sleeves shoved past her elbows, her hair knotted on top of her head with a pencil through it and a pair of plastic tongs in one hand. She comes over and looks up at him under the light, and stops.
“Your eyes are black,” she says. “I’ve been in here since seven looking at you in black and white, and you walk in and it turns out you don’t have any blue in you either.”
“It’s the light.”
“That’s what everybody says about their eyes.” She goes up on her toes and kisses him, her fingers on his jaw smelling of vinegar, and drops back down. “Come look. You’re all over the place.”
He is. Down the line, pinned at the corners, it’s him.

The first one is him asleep. A mattress, a white wall, a man on his back with his face turned toward the lens and one hand tucked under his jaw, his mouth a little open, the St. Michael slid sideways into the hollow of his throat, the sheet down around his hips and his ribs long and pale and bare, with nothing drawn on them at all.
“Monday,” she says. “First light. That’s before the horse. That’s the canvas.”

He never heard the shutter. He looks at the man on the line, who is asleep the way kids sleep in the back seat coming home from a wake, gone, with every door unlocked, and who has no idea anybody is in the room.

The next are from the Point this afternoon, the roll’s last frames, still wet: the back of him walking down into the white water with Tomás’s nine feet of emergency under one arm and the wetsuit rolled to his waist, his shoulders gone white in the print where the sun was on them.
“Still a procession,” Skye says.

After those, the headland for Fenner: the rocks with the white water wrapped around their feet, the old light dark on top, the low wall along the cliff and the cross a small pale mark against it. “Fenner’s,” she says, and moves him on.

Apart from the rest, on a window screen laid across two sawhorses, the dry ones. On top is the swing. Tuesday, the porch, right after Danny’s call, shot through the screen door, so there is a faint grid of mesh over everything. Skye with her head back against the chain, laughing, one bare heel up off the boards. And Jack beside her, turned all the way to her, his mouth open in the middle of a word and the scar in his eyebrow hiked up, looking at her like she has just told him the end of a joke he has been waiting on since grade school.
Ma’s upstairs hall on Glenwood is pictures from the bathroom to the stairs. He has never seen that one.

“Tomás,” Skye says. “He came out with his coffee to tell us to keep it down and stayed for the shot. I didn’t know till the roll came up.” She is looking at the print, not at him. “That face. You don’t do it when anybody’s watching.”
“You took the first one while I was asleep.”
“I did.”
“That’s a little — ”

“That’s why it’s good.” She goes back to the trays and fishes the last of the Point out of the fixer and into the wash, the tongs clicking. “Every picture of me since I was a kid was posed and paid for. Chin down. Give me sad. They want you less tan. I’ve been shot by the best people in the business, and do you know what a camera tells the truth about? Light. Light, and what the client paid.” She pins the print up by one corner and it starts to drip. “These are the first true pictures I’ve ever taken. Because you didn’t know. The only honest thing a camera ever did was catch somebody who wasn’t ready.”
“That’s backwards.”
“Of course it is. You’re here.”

He leans against the dry counter, minding the enlarger, minding Sol. “A true picture’s not one you take. Sixth Station. Every Friday in Lent at St. Brigid’s there’s a plaster woman on the wall with a towel held open in both hands and a face on it. Veronica. She wipes his face on the way up the hill and he leaves it on the cloth. For centuries that’s the picture of him people walked to Rome to see, and she didn’t take it. He gave it to her. They called it the *vera icon*. The true image.” He shrugs. “Her name probably came from the picture, not the other way around. But that’s the idea. True is given.”
“You had to say *probably*.”

“It’s in the contract. Philosophy major. And there’s Guadalupe. A man named Juan Diego opens his cloak in front of a bishop, and roses fall out, and she’s on the inside of it. Nobody painted her. That’s the claim. The Greeks had a word for pictures like that. *Acheiropoieta*. Not made by hands.”
“The lady on the candles at the taquería,” Skye says. “She’s very well lit. I’ll give her that.”

She takes a sheet out of the box and puts the lid back on, and lays the sheet in the easel under the enlarger, and switches the lamp on for a count she keeps under her breath, and off. She slides the blank paper into the developer and rocks the tray with the tongs, slow, a little wave going end to end.
“Watch,” she says. “This is the part nobody takes.”
White paper under the liquid, nothing on it, and nothing, and then a gray where a jaw would be.
“There’s your jaw,” she says, rocking. “There’s the scar. There’s — ”

She stops. The paper goes on without her. His mouth comes up out of the white, closed eyes, the medal in his throat: it’s Monday again, closer, just the face, asleep in a tray of chemicals on Sol’s counter under a red bulb, and Skye stands over it with the tongs in her hand and doesn’t move it on to the next tray.
“So the best picture ever taken,” she says, “nobody took.” She lays the tongs across the end of the tray. “Everything true about anybody is stolen.”

body.text: “You stole me in a den in Montecito. I was reading for a part and you took the grandmother off me.”
body.else: “You stole me in a den in Montecito.”

choices.text: “A true picture’s one somebody gives you.”
response: “A true picture’s one somebody gives you,” he says, and stays on it.
She looks at him across the red. She reaches up and unpins the canvas from the line, him asleep, still dripping, and holds it out. “Then I’m giving you this one.”
“That one’s yours,” he says. “You were up first.”

She keeps it in her hand. She pins it back where it was. From the screen on the sawhorses she takes the swing, dry and curling at one corner, turns it face down on the Formica, and with a grease pencil out of the apron pocket she writes across the back in her capitals while he watches — NOT FOR POSTING — and hands it to him. He opens Hale’s *Moviegoer* to the middle and lays it in between two pages of Hale’s pencil and shuts the book on it.
“Professionally.” She takes a clothespin off the end of the line and clips it to his collar, a price tag.

She lifts the swing off the screen and hands it to him face down. It’s already written on, in grease pencil, in her capitals, a little smeared at the end where her wrist went through it: NOT FOR POSTING.
“I did that at eight,” she says. “Before you knocked. I’m a planner.”
He opens Hale’s *Moviegoer* to the middle and lays it in between two pages of Hale’s pencil and shuts the book on it. The clothespin stays where she put it.
She looks at it on the screen a long time, the mesh over the two of them and the chain and her heel in the air.
“Tomás has an eye,” she says. “Don’t tell him.”
She lifts it off the screen and puts it in his hands face down. “Read the back.”
He tips it to the safelight. Grease pencil, her capitals. “Not for posting.”
“Like you mean it.”
“Not for posting.”
“Good. That’s the caption.” He opens Hale’s *Moviegoer* to the middle and lays it in between two pages of Hale’s pencil and shuts the book on it.

s08a.slug: THURSDAY · 10:20 PM · THE DARKROOM — THE DOOR
body: The record is coming to the end of a side. The print of him asleep is still lying in the developer where she left it, gone darker than she would have let it if she were still printing. She isn’t. She’s been sitting on the edge of the wet counter with her heels against the cabinet, telling him what the skin person in Burbank charges by the hour. “Two hundred dollars to look at my elbows and tell me they’re still elbows. I want that job. I would be so good at that job.” He says the elbows look fine to him. “You’re not licensed,” she says, and hops down.

She puts the lid on the box of paper first. She pushes it to the back of the dry counter, behind the enlarger. She crosses the little room, picks up the gallon jug of fixer from under the sink by its handle, opens the door, and sets the jug against it.

The hall comes in. Not much of it: the dark, and the bass from two streets over louder by half, and at the far end the light over the stove, reaching down the floorboards toward them in a long pale strip. After an hour of red it might as well be noon. It crosses the floor and climbs the side of the wet counter, and in the developer tray the print of him asleep goes gray all at once, and grayer, his face sinking back into it, and then it is a black sheet in a tray with nothing in it.
The prints on the line are fixed. They hang there dripping in the light from the hall, him and him and the headland and him.
“That one was mine anyway,” Skye says.
She stays in the doorway, the stove light down one side of her and the red down the other.
“Why the door?” he says.
“So you know it’s there.”
She leans on the frame with her arms folded and the jug at her ankle, and the bass from two streets over comes down the hall behind her.
He looks at the doorway. It’s a door. It’s a dark hall with a kettle at the end of it.

choices.key: In the darkroom Skye propped the door open on purpose, so you’d know it was there. You shut it.
response: He crosses to it and moves the jug with his foot, and the door swings to on its own weight and takes the hall with it, and the red has the room again.
“Then that’s you,” she says.
She comes back across the room to him. On the turntable the record has run off the end of the side into the groove, and in the shut room the hiss of it going around is suddenly very loud.

choices.key: In the darkroom Skye propped the door open on purpose, so you’d know it was there. You left it open.
response: He leaves it.
“Then we leave it,” she says.
She comes back across the room to him with the stove light on one shoulder and the red on the other, and from then on the hall is a dark doorway behind her with a little of the kitchen in it.

body: The needle rides the run-out groove, a hiss and a small catch, a hiss and a small catch, around and around.

body.text: Behind her the doorway stands open on the dark hall, a little of the stove light lying in it.
body.else: Behind her the door is shut, and a thread of stove light shows along the bottom of it and nowhere else.

body: Skye picks the tongs up off the wet counter and points them at him and drops into a man he hasn’t met — hoarse, two packs a day, a man who has been standing in a field with a bullhorn since before dawn — “Last setup, people. We are losing the — ”
She puts the tongs down.
She takes the apron off over her head and hangs it on its nail. Then she comes to him.

It’s ten-thirty. The van is at five and her flight is at six-forty, and from the first minute she moves like somebody who has done that arithmetic and isn’t going to do it again. She doesn’t hurry. She doesn’t stop, either. She takes Hale’s *Moviegoer* out of his back pocket, with the swing in it, and sets it on the dry counter by the enlarger. She pushes the Carhartt off his shoulders and lets it go, and it lands heavy on the side with the pockets. She gets his T-shirt up and over his head and leaves his arms caught in it while she kisses the middle of his chest beside the medal, and then frees them. She kneels on Sol’s rubber mat and unlaces his boots, both of them, to the last eyelet, and he stands on one foot and then the other like a kid being got ready for church. His belt. His jeans. The rest. He lets her run it.

She stands up in front of him and takes off her own: the T-shirt, the bra, the jeans, the rest, folding nothing, dropping each thing where she stands. The safelight finds her collarbones and the undersides of her breasts and the points of her hips and the long run of her stomach and gives the rest of her to the dark. He has seen all of her by a lamp and in the afternoon and under bathwater and with a parking lot coming through his window. He has never seen her in one color. His hands are shaking. The room is warm; Sol keeps a space heater under the sink for the chemistry.

She walks him backward until the edge of the dry counter is across the small of his back, cold Formica, the enlarger’s column against his wrist, and goes down on her knees on the mat, and takes him in her mouth. Her mouth is hot and the counter is cold and he is caught between the two, and her other hand comes up and spreads on his stomach and holds him back against the Formica, and he lets himself be held.

The red is on her shoulders and in her hair. The knot comes down and the pencil falls out of it and rolls away under the counter, and neither of them goes after it. His hands go into her hair, and then, because he needs somewhere to put them that isn’t her, back to the counter on either side of him, his fingers hooked over the edge. She isn’t slow tonight. She is quick and sure and she knows exactly where he is, every second, and she takes him there fast, his head back against the plywood, the bulb swimming above him, his breath going ragged and then going altogether —
— and she stops.

She takes her mouth away and sits back on her heels with her hand on him, still, and looks up at him in the red with her lips wet and her chin up, and keeps him where he is, right at the edge, with nothing moving. She watches what that does to him. She doesn’t look away from any of it.
He says her name. It arrives in pieces.
“I know,” she says.

She comes up the length of him and kisses him, and he tastes himself in her mouth, and she takes his hand and walks him backward across the room to the daybed and puts him down on Sol’s moving blanket. The iron rail is cold against his shoulders. The blanket smells like the back of a truck.

She turns around above him. She puts a knee on either side of his shoulders and settles her hips down to his mouth, and bends over him and takes him into her mouth again, and for the first time it isn’t anybody’s turn.

Every other night it has been one of them and then the other: somebody giving and somebody getting, somebody saying what they want and somebody doing it. Now it’s both at once, and there is no room in him to think about her and be thought about at the same time, so he stops trying to think. He has her thighs in his hands, the backs of them trembling under his palms. He has the taste of her, salt and sharp, and the heat of her against his face, and the sound she makes going straight down into him so that he feels it more than hears it, and his own going up into her, and her hair spilling over his hips, and her heels pressing into the blanket on either side of his head. It is too much to do both, and they do both.

When he gets close she is ahead of him. She lifts her mouth off him and holds still, her cheek on his hip, breathing hard against his skin, and when he groans her name at the ceiling she says into his hip, “We’ve got till five,” and waits until he has come back down; and starts again. The second time it happens he feels her smile against him. The third time he understands what she is doing. So when her thighs start to shake against his ears and her hips start chasing his mouth, he eases off, slows, holds her there, and her fist comes down on the blanket by his knee, and the sound she makes into him is half complaint and half yes. And he starts again. She showed him, and he learns, and after that it is the two of them holding each other right at the edge and not letting either one over, again and again, until he has lost count of whose edge it is.

Overhead, the prints have been dripping the whole time. One lets go a fat cold drop off its corner — the back of him, walking into the Pacific — and it lands between her shoulder blades. She jerks, and laughs. It bursts out of her, loud and sudden, with her mouth open, and she claps a hand over it out of habit, and then takes the hand away, because there is no Doug in this house, no cinderblock, nobody on the other side of these walls but the yard and the fence and the drop to the beach. She laughs out loud into Sol’s darkroom. Another drop hits his shin, and that sets her off again.
“Your face is dripping on me,” she says, when she can.
“You hung it there.”
“I hung it there,” she agrees, and puts her mouth back on him, still laughing, so that he feels the laugh too.

When she has her breath she turns around and comes up the length of him, skin on skin from his knees to his mouth, and lies along him, and her hair comes down around both their faces. Her back is wet with print water under his hands and cold, and she is hot everywhere else. The St. Michael is caught under her, pressed into his breastbone by her weight.
“I know what I said about the morning,” she says. “I’m changing it. It’s mine.”

body.text: “Tuesday you told me to ask you. I wouldn’t take it like that. I’m asking now.”
“Tuesday you said you didn’t know if you’d say no. I didn’t want to find out on your floor.”
“Tuesday you held me and talked about the swing. I let you.”
“Tuesday you said no before I could choose.”

body: Her mouth is close enough that he feels the words land. “I want you inside me, Jack. Tonight. In here. Before anybody has to go anywhere.”
She says it and waits.

The needle goes around in its groove. Over her shoulder, on the line, he is asleep with his ribs bare, dripping. Somewhere in him the front half of a Hail Mary starts up out of habit, the way it does at red lights and in hospital hallways, and doesn’t get past *full of*. Every no he has ever said to her, he said to this face. He looks up at it in the red, close enough to feel her breathe, and waits to hear what he’s going to say.

choices.key: In the darkroom Skye asked, in so many words. You said yes.
response: “Yes,” he says.
It sounds the same in red as it would in any light. Her breath goes out of her against his mouth, and her forehead comes down to his and stays.

choices.key: In the darkroom Skye asked. You answered by taking off your St. Michael and laying it on the counter.
response: He gets a hand in under her and lifts his confirmation medal over his head. The chain catches on his ear, and he works it free, and reaches past her off the edge of the daybed as far as his arm goes, to the dry counter by the enlarger, and lays it there.
The small sound of it on the Formica. She turns her head and watches it go down.

choices.key: In the darkroom Skye asked. You answered with her real name: Mary Catherine.
response: “Mary Catherine,” he says.

response.text: She has heard him say it once before, in 412, with his grandmother’s sentence still on it — *a good name for a wife* — and he watches that sentence come back into her face in the red.
response.else: Her face, in the red, at her own name.

response: “Yes,” she says for him, as if he’d asked.

choices.key: In the darkroom Skye asked. You got as far as ‘wait’ — and she had already stopped.
response: “Skye — wait — ”

He gets as far as her name and the front of the next word, and finds she has gone still above him, her hand already closed around the St. Michael on its chain. Whatever he was going to say, she was there before it.
